theme: The better covenant; the better sacrifice
readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 8:1-9:28. This is the theological heart of the letter. Look for the contrast between the earthly tent and the heavenly one, and between the blood of animals and the blood of Christ. Read the quotation of Jeremiah 31:31-34 in 8:8-12 carefully. You encountered it earlier in this plan on the covenant day.
settingTheScene: The author has argued that Christ is a priest of a better order. Now he states the main point: we have such a high priest, who is seated in heaven, and he serves in a better sanctuary under a better covenant. This section is where the language of Hebrews becomes most temple-centered, and it can feel unfamiliar. But the author is working with the elements his readers knew well: the tabernacle, the Day of Atonement, and the blood of sacrifices. He shows that these were copies and shadows, and that Christ has entered the reality. This is the heart of how the old covenant fits with the new.
observation: The main point: we have a high priest who is seated at the right hand of the throne in heaven (8:1).
The earthly priests serve “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (8:5).
Christ has obtained a ministry “as much more excellent” as the covenant he mediates is better, “enacted on better promises” (8:6).
Jeremiah 31:31-34 is quoted in full, with its promise of a new covenant, laws on hearts, and sins remembered no more (8:8-12).
“In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete” (8:13).
The first tent had its furnishings, and only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (9:1-7).
The Holy Spirit signified that the way into the holy places was not yet opened (9:8).
“Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (9:22). Christ appeared “once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (9:26).
interpretation:
The language of copy and shadow is crucial. The author does not say the tabernacle was a mistake. It was designed by God, built according to the pattern shown to Moses. But a pattern is not the thing itself. A shadow tells you something real about the object that casts it, but you cannot embrace a shadow. The tabernacle taught Israel that God is holy, that sin is serious, that blood is needed, and that a mediator must stand between God and humanity. All of that was true. But it could not permanently deal with sin.

Chapter 8 then quotes Jeremiah’s promise, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament. God says the days are coming when he will make a new covenant. Its features are striking. The law will be written on hearts. Everyone will know the LORD, from the least to the greatest. And God will remember sins no more. The author’s comment is quietly devastating: by speaking of a “new” covenant, God has marked the old one as obsolete and ready to vanish. The old covenant did not fail because God failed. Jeremiah 31:32 says Israel broke it. The new covenant is better because it deals with the heart problem that the old one could only expose.

Chapter 9 describes the day of atonement in detail. Once a year, the high priest entered the Most Holy Place carrying blood for himself and the people. The Holy Spirit was teaching something by this arrangement: the way into God’s presence was not yet open. The curtain remained. The sacrifices could cleanse the outside, providing ceremonial purity, but they could not clear the conscience.

Then the contrast arrives in verse 11: “But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come…” He entered not an earthly tent but the heavenly sanctuary, not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own blood. And he did so once for all, securing an eternal redemption. If the blood of animals could sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God. The cleansing is deeper because the sacrifice is greater.

The author uses a legal image in verses 16-17. A covenant is like a will. It takes effect when the one who made it dies. Christ’s death put the new covenant into effect, and he mediates its promised inheritance to those who are called.

The chapter ends with a striking picture. Humans die once and then face judgment, so Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him. The first coming dealt with sin. The second will bring salvation in its fullness.
connection: This chapter draws on Exodus 25-40, Leviticus 16 (the Day of Atonement), and Jeremiah 31:31-34, which you studied on the covenant day earlier. The blood of the covenant echoes Exodus 24:8, and Jesus used the same language at the Last Supper in Luke 22:20. The “second appearing” links to Acts 1:11, the ascension passage, and to Titus 2:13.
application:
First, let verse 14 reach your conscience. If you still carry guilt over sins God has forgiven, remember that Christ’s blood does not just cover the past. It cleanses the conscience. Confess what is true, and then rest in what is done.

Second, notice the promise that God’s law is written on hearts. If you have felt that obedience is a burden, ask the Holy Spirit to make God’s commands your delight, as he promised.

Third, take comfort in the phrase “once for all.” There is no sacrifice left for you to make to earn forgiveness. Serve God because you are cleansed, not to become clean.

Fourth, live in expectation. Christ will appear a second time. Ask yourself how your week would change if you were eagerly waiting for him.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the new covenant sealed with the blood of his Son.
Ask him to cleanse your conscience from dead works.
Ask him to write his law on your heart.
